newsitem.title: USA: Consumer prices modest in May, factories humming.
newsitem.headline: Consumer prices modest in May, factories humming.

text.p: Cheaper gasoline and lower air fares helped keep consumer prices in check during May, the Labor Department said on Tuesday, while factories churned out more new cars and other manufactured goods.

A series of reports from the government and the Federal Reserve suggested the economy continued to grow steadily, if at a slowing pace, with inflation muted enough to likely head off any imminent increases in interest rates.

The Consumer Price Index edged up only 0.1 percent for the third consecutive month in May, a tame rise following on the heels of last Friday's report showing wholesale prices dropped for the fifth straight month in May.
Separately, the Federal Reserve said industrial output rose solidly last month by 0.4 percent after a 0.3 percent April gain.
The rate at which factories operated crept up to 83.7 percent in May from 83.6 percent in April. It was the highest capacity use in more than 1-1/2 years since 83.9 percent in September 1995.

Still, analysts said the reports demonstrated the economy's ability to grow at a healthy clip without sparking inflation and saw little reason for Federal Reserve policy-makers to boost interest rates at their next meeting July 1-2.

A third report from the Commerce Department showed the construction rate for new homes and apartments fell for a third straight month in May, down 4.8 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.397 million.

That followed revised declines of 0.7 percent in April and 4.8 percent in March as builders pulled back after a surge in construction activity at the beginning of the year when the weather was exceptionally mild.

The reports fit with predictions that second-quarter economic expansion, while solid, likely will slow to less than half the sizzling 5.8 percent annual rate posted during the first three months this year.

"Today's reports are good indicators of conditions for the rest of the year," said Jerry Jasinowski, president of the National Association of Manufacturers. "Industrial growth is continuing at a stable pace, while inflation remains low."
White House officials said the economic expansion remained on firm footing after more than six years of unbroken growth and was slowing in line with expectations.

"Overall, the data ... paint a picture of an economy that has slowed from the blistering pace of the first quarter to a sustainable pace in the second," said Janet Yellen, chairwoman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers.

Financial markets first nosedived on the reports, with the Dow Jones industrial average plummeting before recovering to post a gain of about 9 points at 7,763 in late trading. Bond prices fell sharply but recouped some of their losses later.

The CPI report was encouraging, with the so-called "core" rate after stripping out often-volatile food and energy costs up just 0.2 percent last month after a 0.3 percent gain in April. Gasoline prices fell 4.1 percent, their biggest drop since a 4.6 percent plunge in March 1991 as the last recession was ending.
So far this year the CPI has risen at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.4 percent, less than half the 3.3 percent increase recorded for all of 1996.

Energy prices overall declined 2.4 percent in May after falling 1.5 percent during April. Airline fares fell 1.3 percent while automobile finance charges declined 2.5 percent, the biggest drop since a 2.8 percent slide in February 1992.

The Commerce Department report on home building showed housing starts fell 4.8 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.397 million in May after declines of 0.7 percent in April and 4.8 percent in March.
"Special factors, especially favorable weather conditions, crowded more of 1997's home building into the year's early months," said economist Ken Mayland of KeyCorp in Cleveland.
But falling mortgage rates and plentiful jobs are expected to provide a firm floor under the housing sector, keeping it from becoming a weak spot for the economy.

The Fed's report on industrial output said the end of a strike against General Motors Corp. in May fostered increased assembly rates for new cars and trucks. Demand was steady for new commercial aircraft and manufacturing of high-technology goods from appliances to computers was brisk.
Mining production increased 2 percent in May -- partly because electrical utilities were restocking their inventories of coal -- after falling 0.5 percent in April.
But utilities output dropped 1.9 percent following a 2.3 percent jump in April, in part because relatively cool weather reduced the need for air conditioning.
